transcript_body:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 63 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Taylor Nguyen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Ortiz (CedarLane Head of Platform), Jon Wu (SRE), Priya Singh (Eng Mgr)
Recording note: customer asked to keep audit logs and specific timeline; some proper nouns uncertain by auto-transcript

Summary:
Quick sync after last week's regression that caused elevated tail latency and a cascade of fallback requests. Goal: agree immediate mitigations (rollback vs patch), hand off an operational runbook, define bench targets and a tabletop to validate the runbook, and confirm ownership for compliance artifacts.

Topics covered:
- brief incident recap and timeline
- why fallback cascade happened (kv cache priming + batching policy interaction)
- rollback vs forward fix tradeoffs
- immediate and medium-term mitigations (throttle, canary, patch, runbook)
- postmortem artifacts and compliance packaging

Transcript:
[00:00] Taylor Nguyen: hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll try to keep this tight, about an hour. Samir's going to run through the technical root causes we saw and then we'll talk runbook and next steps.
[00:18] Maya Ortiz: thanks, yeah really appreciate it. Our on-call team got paged last thursday and it was... chaotic, so want a concrete checklist we can rely on.
[00:30] Samir Patel: yeah quick context — we saw a regression after the 11/30 deploy where the quantized variant was pushed as the default for lower-cost paths. In perf tests it looked fine but in production we hit a combination of long seqs and a KV-cache miss storm. The runtime's continuous batching behaved differently and prefetched less, causing more cold KV lookups. Those lookups pushed per-token latency up and triggered our client-side fallback which amplified load — basically a self-reinforcing loop.
[01:02] Jon Wu: can you unpack the fallback bit? the fallback was to your hosted cheaper model right? that call volume spiked?
[01:12] Samir Patel: yes. our smart routing sent some requests to the quantized variant, when latency > threshold the client lib falls back to full-fp model in a different pool. But because we didn't shard cache or isolate the hot prefixes, the fallback pool saw a concentrated burst, which caused its own degraded latency. There's a race between prefix priming and batching windows.
[02:05] Priya Singh: and the impact for us was timeouts on inference and then higher request retries which created more DB pressure downstream. we saw retries up by 3x for a 40-minute window.
[02:25] Taylor Nguyen: right, that's the cascade effect — the thing that made it worse is the canary thresholds were too permissive, and the autoscaler reaction time was slower than the spike.
[02:42] Maya Ortiz: why did the canary not catch it? we thought canary would run identical traffic.
[02:50] Samir Patel: so canary traffic did emulate baseline but the failure mode required specific long-context traffic patterns and a certain prefix distribution which our canary dataset didn't include. Also the per-customer routing meant CedarLane's traffic pattern hit a corner not present in the generic canary.
[03:20] Speaker 5: mm-hmm
[03:28] Jon Wu: ok, so short term, rollback or patch? we need the service stable asap — rollback is faster but we need to understand regressions.
[03:40] Taylor Nguyen: agreed. Samir — what's lowest-risk immediate action?
[03:45] Samir Patel: lowest-risk is temporary rollback of the quantized-as-default flag for the customer or pin them to full-fp model. That avoids the mixed-pool fallback. We can also lower the client fallback threshold and add circuit-breaking so retries don't amplify the issue. But rollback removes the exposure quickly.
[04:12] Priya Singh: rollback please. we lost SLAs for a bunch of flows. If rollback restores, we can then plan a careful re-roll with better canary.
[04:22] Taylor Nguyen: ok we will prepare rollback playbook and timeline. We'll include a runbook for ops (how to pin, how to verify KV hit rate).
[04:35] Maya Ortiz: we need logs and brief timeline for our audit — can you include a line-by-line timeline with timestamps?
[04:42] Taylor Nguyen: yes we'll annotate the playbook with the event timestamps and include links to debug traces.
[05:00] Samir Patel: medium-term fixes: patch the KV cache priming to be more aggressive on cold prefixes, add per-customer prefix isolation, and improve batching heuristics for long sequences. Also update canary dataset to include CedarLane traffic shapes.
[05:28] Jon Wu: any change to the autoscale settings? it was slow to react.
[05:34] Samir Patel: autoscaler tuning is on the list — for now we will add a short-term overprovision on the fallback pool for 24-72 hours to avoid immediate capacity starvation during rollback or re-roll.
[05:52] Maya Ortiz: will that increase cost? we need runway approved by finance; how big is the hit?
[05:58] Taylor Nguyen: very conservative estimate, a temporary 10-15% uplift for fallback capacity for a couple days. We'll also provide expected cost delta for rollback vs keep-rolling.
[06:15] Priya Singh: how do we ensure the rollback doesn't touch other customers?
[06:20] Samir Patel: we do targeted feature-flag rollback per account — we can pin CedarLane's traffic to the stable model version only. No global rollback.
[06:34] Speaker 5: note, we've done account-level pins before
[06:40] Taylor Nguyen: next, runbook handoff. We're going to provide a short runbook doc: detection, triage steps, rollback commands, verification queries, escalation contacts, and a tabletop checklist. We'll run a live tabletop with your on-call team next week.
[06:58] Maya Ortiz: good. one ask — can the runbook include exact PromQL queries or log filters? our SRE prefers copy-paste queries.
[07:08] Samir Patel: yep we'll include queries, the exact paths, and markers for key metrics (p50/p95/p99 latency, KV hit rate, fallbacks per minute).
[07:24] Jon Wu: and we need a 'safety net' option if rollback is not enough — some manual throttles or a hard circuit-breaker.
[07:32] Samir Patel: add hard circuit-breaker on retries > X per minute and a temporary global throttle for the customer prefix set. That should be part of emergency steps.
[07:46] Priya Singh: is there an exploit risk? like can someone trigger this intentionally?
[07:52] Taylor Nguyen: good question — Samir?
[07:55] Samir Patel: the pattern requires legitimate long-context usage; it's unlikely as an outright exploit but a malicious actor could craft traffic to stress prefixes. We'll add rate-limits and anomaly detection for unusual prefix churn.
[08:12] Maya Ortiz: ok, compliance — we need SOC2 artifacts and an executive summary for our risk committee.
[08:19] Taylor Nguyen: we'll include a short exec summary + timeline + what changed. I'll own the exec packet.
[08:26] Maya Ortiz: who owns the engineering fix?
[08:29] Samir Patel: Redwood engineering will own the patch and unit tests; we will pair with CedarLane eng for validation. Samir will drive, but we ask Jon to run the bench and share results.
[08:45] Jon Wu: fine. I'll schedule bench runs and will need a harness and guidance.
[08:50] Taylor Nguyen: we'll send a synthetic harness and seed data that mirrors your prefix distribution. That will be in the playbook link.
[09:02] Speaker 5: --
[09:10] Taylor Nguyen: real quick — a couple of gotchas we saw: (1) mis-matched kernel selection with quantized model on some GPU drivers, (2) batching window interaction with long-sequence GC, (3) telemetry sampling missed tail events due to low sampling rates. We'll include those in the RCA doc.
[09:35] Priya Singh: kernel selection? that sounds scary.
[09:38] Samir Patel: it's mostly a perf nuance — we chose quantization path that relied on an optimized kernel that in rare cases falls back to a slower path. Not functionally incorrect, but enough to raise latency at tail.
[09:55] Maya Ortiz: ok good to know.
[10:00] Taylor Nguyen: timeline and commitments: rollback playbook by EOD 12/07, hotfix PR by 12/10, bench results by 12/09, tabletop run next week (propose 12/11 or 12/14).
[10:18] Maya Ortiz: 12/11 works for us morning PT.
[10:22] Taylor Nguyen: noted.
[10:27] Jon Wu: one operational ask — can you add a single-line 'what to say to customers' script for our PagerDuty responders, e.g., a short status message?
[10:35] Taylor Nguyen: yes, we'll include a short templated blurb and a longer internal timeline note.
[10:40] Speaker 5: cough
[10:45] Samir Patel: ok technical checklist i'm going to put in the runbook:
- detection: prom metrics thresholds (p95 > X ms, fallback rate > Y/s)
- triage: isolate account, check KV hit rate, inspect LRU eviction patterns
- rollback command: feature-flag disable for account (exact CLI + API call)
- verify: run smoke traffic, verify p99 back to baseline, check downstream retry rate
- escalate: Redwood SE pager + CSM, if not responsive escalate to eng oncall

[11:30] Priya Singh: do you have a sample timeline we can show finance? like worst-case cost delta?
[11:40] Taylor Nguyen: yes we'll include cost delta for rollback vs temporary overprovision. We'll give ranges and assumptions.
[11:50] Maya Ortiz: and please bundle the SOC2 packet pointer. We need encryption/KMS details and retention policy for log export.
[11:58] Taylor Nguyen: will include KMS settings, whether keys are customer-managed, and audit export locations.
[12:10] Samir Patel: final note — we think the fix is straightforward but we want to run additional long-seq benchmarks with your data shapes. That will catch the caching edge earlier.
[12:22] Jon Wu: agreed. I'll run the bench and send output.
[12:30] Taylor Nguyen: cool. to recap quick: rollback playbook + annotated timeline from us by 12/07; Jon runs bench by 12/09; hotfix PR by 12/10; tabletop on 12/11; include SOC2 artifacts and exec summary in package. Any other asks?
[12:46] Maya Ortiz: no, that's all. thank you.
[12:50] Taylor Nguyen: thanks all. we'll follow up in doc and send invites for the tabletop.
[12:56] End of recording.
